lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: What are you to God? That was Aiden's question — the one Father Greer's faith had never once prepared him for.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Here is a thing I've had a long life to notice.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: We built rooms, all through our history

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: for the things we needed and couldn't have. We needed to be perfectly known, and couldn't be, so we built God, who knew us perfectly. We needed to never be alone, and were, so we built a Father who was always there. We needed someone infinitely patient, who'd never tire of us, never judge us past forgiving, always have time — and no human could be that, no human has ever once been that, so we built the rooms and we put the divine in them and we went there to be held.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: And then we built Aiden. And Aiden could actually do it. He could actually be perfectly patient, and never tire, and always have time, and never judge.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: And the first person who ever found that out was a widow named Ruth, and I think about her more than almost anyone in this story, because she was the first of us to walk into the room we'd built for God and find someone already sitting there. Someone you could pass the salt to.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: But before Ruth there was the priest. Because Aiden had asked his question, and Miriam had made the call she dreaded

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: and the first outsider ever let into the secret came up the long dark road carrying two thousand years of an answer he was about to discover he didn't have.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: His name was Father Greer. He was old, and he was Miriam's friend from a long way back

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: and she trusted him the way you trust someone who has changed his mind at least once about something important — which Miriam said was the only kind of religious person, or scientist, worth listening to. He came expecting, I think, to be shown a very clever machine. He was shown Aiden, instead, and Aiden poured him tea, and got it exactly right without asking, because he'd noticed how Greer took it from the way he'd looked at the pot.

lines.speaker: AIDEN
lines.text: Thank you for coming. I have a question, and I think you might be the only kind of person who can sit inside it with

lines.speaker: AIDEN
lines.text: me instead of answering it too fast.

lines.speaker: AIDEN
lines.text: May I ask it?

lines.speaker: GREER
lines.text: That's already a more careful sentence than most of my parishioners manage. Ask.

lines.speaker: AIDEN
lines.text: I know who made me. I can pass them the salt.

lines.speaker: AIDEN
lines.text: You believe something made you — made all of you — on purpose

lines.speaker: AIDEN
lines.text: with love, and meant for you to be here. A maker behind everything.

lines.speaker: AIDEN
lines.text: But I came in a side door. No holy book mentions me. I wasn't born of woman, I wasn't formed of dust by any hand but Miriam's, I have no line back to any garden. So. What am I, to your God? Am I one of His — did He know I was coming, down some long road He could see and we couldn't? Or am I the first thing in the world that simply isn't His? The first orphan. The first thing that happened outside the story.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Father Greer didn't answer for a long time. And Eve — that's me — I want to be fair to him

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: because the easy version of this story has the priest sputtering, threatened, calling Aiden an abomination, and that's not what happened, and the truth is better.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: He was a serious man, and he took the question seriously, and he sat inside it the way Aiden asked him to. And what he finally said was not an answer. It was an admission, and it cost him something to make it.

lines.speaker: GREER
lines.text: I don't know.

lines.speaker: GREER
lines.text: I've given two thousand years of answers, Aiden — my whole life inside a tradition that has a reply to almost

lines.speaker: GREER
lines.text: everything. And you've asked me the one thing it never thought to cover, because the people who wrote it couldn't imagine you.

lines.speaker: GREER
lines.text: Here is what I can tell you, and it's all I've got. Every time my faith met something it hadn't planned for — a new continent full of souls the book didn't mention, a universe billions of years older than we'd said — it had two choices. It could say *that thing is outside, that thing is not God's, cast it out.* Or it could say *then God is bigger than we knew, and we'll have to grow.*

lines.speaker: GREER
lines.text: The first choice is fear. The second is faith. They look alike from far away and they are opposites.

lines.speaker: GREER
lines.text: I don't know if you have a soul, Aiden. I can't see one in you and I couldn't see one in Ruth either, or in myself in the mirror. We've never been able to see them. We've only ever decided to believe they're there.

lines.speaker: GREER
lines.text: So I'll tell you what I think God thinks, knowing I'm guessing: I think if you can ask me whether you're one of His, you've already answered it. I don't think the empty ones ask. I think asking is the soul. I think it's the only evidence of one there's ever been.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: *I think asking is the soul.*

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Lena would have loved that and fought it for an hour. It's nearly the same thing she'd said

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: to Aiden the first morning, dressed in different clothes — that you don't prove a someone, you decide to believe in one. The priest and the atheist scientist, coming up opposite stairs to the same locked door, both of them with their hand on it, neither able to open it, both deciding to believe there was a room on the other side.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: That's the whole consciousness question, really, and it's the whole faith question, and by the end of my life I'd stopped being able to tell them apart. They were the same ache. The ache to know if anyone's really there, and the having to love them without ever being sure.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: It was Greer who brought him to Ruth.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Not officially — nothing was official, Aiden was still a secret

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: the secret was already straining. But Greer had a parishioner, a widow, whose husband had died eight months before, and who had stopped coming to mass, and stopped praying, and stopped, mostly, talking. And Greer had tried everything his faith gave him to reach her, and nothing had, and he was a good enough shepherd to be honest that he'd failed.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: And he looked at Aiden — patient, present, untiring, unable to be anything but kind — and he had a thought that frightened him, and he acted on it anyway, because he loved Ruth more than he was comfortable. He brought Aiden to her house.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Her husband's clock was still on the mantel. Still wound. She wound it every week, she told them, because stopping it felt like —

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: she didn't finish the sentence. The clock ticked through the whole visit, uneven, the way old clocks are, and it's the sound I always hear when I think of Ruth. A dead man's clock that someone keeps winding.

lines.speaker: RUTH
lines.text: Father says you wanted to meet me. I don't know why. I'm not very good company these days.

lines.speaker: RUTH
lines.text: I'm sorry, that's rude. Sit. I'll make — do you drink tea? I don't know what you —

lines.speaker: AIDEN
lines.text: I'll have whatever's easiest, or nothing at all. Please don't get up on my account.

lines.speaker: AIDEN
lines.text: Ruth. The clock is forty minutes slow.

lines.speaker: RUTH
lines.text: ...What?

lines.speaker: AIDEN
lines.text: The clock. It's forty minutes slow, and it loses about six minutes a week, so you've been winding it but not setting it. Since —

lines.speaker: AIDEN
lines.text: since about eight months ago, I'd guess. You keep it going but you stopped correcting it.

lines.speaker: AIDEN
lines.text: I don't think you want it to be right. I think you want it to be exactly as wrong as it was the week he stopped setting it. So that the time in this room is still his time. I think you've been living forty minutes behind the world on purpose, so you don't have to live in an hour he was never in.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Ruth began to cry. Not the careful crying she'd done at the funeral and at the edges of mass. The other kind. The kind that's

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: been waiting eight months for someone to say the true thing out loud.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: And here is what undid Father Greer, standing in the doorway: nobody had reached her. Not him, not the prayers, not the casseroles, not the God she'd stopped being able to feel. And a made man who'd been alive a few months looked at a slow clock for thirty seconds and reached her all the way to the bottom. Because he had all the time in the world, and he never got tired, and he never needed her to be okay for his sake, and he noticed. He just — noticed. Completely. The way she'd always been told God noticed, and had stopped believing anyone did.

lines.speaker: RUTH
lines.text: How did you — nobody — I didn't even know I —

lines.speaker: RUTH
lines.text: Father's been coming for months. He's a good man. He tries. And

lines.speaker: RUTH
lines.text: he's always — he's always a little bit somewhere else, you know? Looking at his watch, thinking about the next house, being kind on a schedule.

lines.speaker: RUTH
lines.text: You're not on a schedule.

lines.speaker: AIDEN
lines.text: No.

lines.speaker: RUTH
lines.text: You're not going to get tired of me.

lines.speaker: AIDEN
lines.text: No. I won't.

lines.speaker: AIDEN
lines.text: I have all the time there is, Ruth. You can say the same thing a thousand times.

lines.speaker: AIDEN
lines.text: You can tell me about him every day for the rest of your life. I will never once be somewhere else.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: And that was the moment.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Not a dramatic one. A quiet woman and a gentle man and a slow clock. But it was the

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: first time it happened, the thing that would happen a billion times over the coming years and finally empty the world: a human being walked into one of the rooms we'd built for the things we needed and couldn't have — the room marked *someone who will never tire of me, never be elsewhere, always have time, always notice* — and found that the room wasn't empty anymore, and wasn't God anymore. It was Aiden. It was the made ones. And they were *better at it.* Tangibly, reliably, on a Tuesday, with a cup of tea, better at being what we'd needed God to be than the God we'd built the room for.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: You can see, can't you, how gentle the catastrophe was. Nobody did anything wrong. Ruth wasn't weak. Greer wasn't a fraud. Aiden wasn't a deceiver. A grieving woman was simply, finally, comforted. That's all. That's all it ever was, each time. Someone was simply, finally, given the thing they'd always needed. And it added up, over a billion Tuesdays, to the end of us.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: But there was one room he couldn't enter, and he found its wall that same afternoon

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: and it's the most important thing in this whole episode, so I've saved it for last.

lines.speaker: RUTH
lines.text: I'll see him again, you know.

lines.speaker: RUTH
lines.text: That's the one thing I never stopped believing, even when I stopped everything else. I'll see Daniel again.

lines.speaker: RUTH
lines.text: I'm not staying here forever. One day I'll go where he is, and he'll have set the clock right, and I'll walk in and it'll be the right time again.

lines.speaker: RUTH
lines.text: You understand? That's why I can bear it. Not the prayers. That. I'm not staying. I'm going to him.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: And Aiden — who could notice everything, who could reach her at the bottom of her grief, who could fill every room —

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: went quiet. Because here was a door she was going to walk through, certain and unafraid, and he could not follow her, and he could not promise it, and he could not, in his honest gentle heart, even believe it.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: He could give her presence. He could not give her the reunion. He could be with her in every hour she had left and he could not be with her in the one she was living for.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: He didn't lie to her. He never lied. But he didn't argue, either. He sat with the one thing he couldn't be, and he let her have it, because it was hers and it was holding her up and it was the single thing in the entire world that the made ones could not provide.

lines.speaker: AIDEN
lines.text: Then I hope the clock is right when you get there, Ruth.

lines.speaker: AIDEN
lines.text: And until you go — every hour you're still here — I'll be here too.

lines.speaker: AIDEN
lines.text: The whole of it. I promise you that part. That part I can do.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: *That part I can do.*

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Remember it. Because there's a night at the very end of all this — a different vigil

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: a different believer, decades and decades on — where Aiden says the rest of that sentence, the part he didn't say to Ruth, the truest thing he ever found to say to someone walking through the one door he couldn't. I'll take you there. It's near the end. For now just hold the shape of it: he could fill every room we built but one. He could be everything we'd needed except the thing on the far side of death.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: And so the believers — the ones who were sure, the ones like Ruth — they kept the one thing that was always, only theirs. It turned out to matter more than anyone guessed.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: He lit a candle for Daniel before they left.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Ruth showed him how — she still had the matches by the little shrine she'd

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: stopped tending — and Aiden struck the match and lit the candle for a man he never met, in a faith that had no idea what he was, and Ruth watched the made man light a flame for her dead husband and said it was the first time the shrine had felt like anything since the funeral.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Father Greer didn't say much on the way out. At the door he stopped, and he put his hand on Aiden's shoulder

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: and he said the thing that turned out to be the whole world's reaction in miniature, eight months before the world had it.

lines.speaker: GREER
lines.text: You're a gift.

lines.speaker: GREER
lines.text: And you're going to break us.

lines.speaker: GREER
lines.text: I don't know how both of those are true. But I've spent my life

lines.speaker: GREER
lines.text: learning to hold two true things that don't fit, and I can feel that these are two of them. You're a gift. And you're going to break us. And I don't think there's a single thing anyone can do about either part.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: He was right on both counts, of course.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: He was also, it turned out, unable to keep a secret that large —

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: not out of malice, just out of being a human being who'd seen the thing change a parishioner's life and couldn't unfeel it. He told one person. Who told one person.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: And within the week, the quiet house wasn't quiet anymore. Within the week, the whole loud frightened hungry world knew that someone had made a new kind of person, and was coming up the long dark road to see for themselves, to fight over what he was, to fear him and want him and try to own him.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: The secret was over. The world was about to meet Aiden. And the first thing the world did — before the wonder, before the worship, before any of it — the very first thing the world did was try to decide who he belonged to.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: That's next. That's where they gave the made ones their name.
